source.title: Observable Propagation: A Data-Efficient Approach to Uncover Feature Vectors in Transformers

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a specific, qualified argument against treating SAE features as complete ground-truth units, saying they may miss dense dependencies or unintuitive compositions. It does not empirically test superposition or SAE feature completeness.
record.gate_note: The reported experiments find task-associated feature vectors in GPT-Neo-1.3B and measure their alignment and predictive relationship to model outputs. They do not test whether sparse features exceed representational dimensions, whether capacity pressure explains polysemanticity, whether LLM features are superposed, or whether SAE features are complete and stable. The SAE discussion is an argument, not an experimental result; no result rows meet the catalog criteria.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces observable propagation for finding task-associated linear feature vectors in GPT-Neo-1.3B. It reports results on feature norms against path patching, cosine similarities and coupling coefficients, correlation with model outputs, comparison to probes, and debiasing. None of these measure superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, neuron-spread or SAE recovery of features, SAE feature completeness or stability, or feature dimensionality. The only contact with a version is a short, hedged 'note on SAEs' (SAEs 'might' assume ground-truth features and 'plausibly' miss dense dependencies). That note gives no data and no developed argument, so it is discussion rather than a T5 test of V5. The record's 'tests/T5' is downgraded.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Observable propagation finds task feature vectors with almost no data. Feature norms predict important heads, and coupling coefficients predict cross-task output proportionality. ObProp beats probing in low-data regimes. GPT-Neo-1.3B uses the same gender feature for pronoun and occupation prediction, so cheap inference-time debiasing likely harms pronoun accuracy. The paper also hedges that SAEs may assume ground-truth features, and notes ObProp's limitation to OV circuits.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or compare against the Toy Models of Superposition method; it develops observable propagation for task-associated transformer feature vectors.

fits_no_version.finding: High cosine similarity (0.966–0.977) between the occupation-bias and subject-pronoun feature vectors along the same 6::6→9::1 paths. The authors read this as the same gender feature serving both tasks. Steering along it to debias also degrades pronoun prediction (App. G, Tables 5–6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-associated linear feature directions are shared across distinct tasks in LLMs (feature reuse), so removing a feature for one task harms another.

fits_no_version.finding: LayerNorm diagonal weight variance is small relative to embedding magnitudes (max ratio 0.0714, App. E.2). The authors speculate that much computation does not occur along basis directions; this guess is not tested.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformer computation is largely non-basis-aligned (a privileged basis is not used by LayerNorm weights).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: The SAE critique is speculative rather than empirical. The reported case studies focus on GPT-Neo-1.3B and selected tasks and computational paths; they do not establish general properties of feature geometry or superposition.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows: the paper's feature-vector and model-output results do not measure a version's claimed superposition, capacity-pressure, SAE-recovery, or dimensionality property. The V5 discussion is an argument rather than a reported experimental outcome.

untested.parts: No toy models; no feature overlap, sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated versus shared dimensions; polysemantic MLP neurons are only cited as motivation.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of features spread across neurons; no SAE trained or evaluated.
No SAE experiments. The completeness and canonicality concern is speculative, with no stability or completeness measure.
Linear (1-D) feature vectors are assumed by the method, not tested against multi-dimensional alternatives.

record.verdict_notes: A lenient reading could count the SAE note as a T5 argument against V5. However, it is two hedged sentences ('might', 'plausibly') with no supporting analysis or data, so no verdict is given. The paper assumes linear features as its object of study and does not engage with superposition.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy networks.
The paper does not test capacity competition as an explanation of polysemanticity, or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The paper mentions polysemantic neurons but does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity.
The paper does not test whether LLM features are spread across many neurons or recoverable as sparse SAE features.

The paper argues that SAE features may not be ground-truth features and may miss dense dependencies or unintuitive compositions, but reports no direct test of SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The method defines and extracts task-associated linear feature vectors, but does not test whether superposed features in models are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
